1:
The name is the first thing noticed. Gill observes that it is the same as Joshua and Jesus and signifies a saviour, and that the prophet was in some things a type of Christ the Saviour, prophesying of him and being himself an instrument of saving men, as all true prophets were. Henry says the same and draws the lesson, that prophets and faithful ministers help to save many a soul from death by saving it from sin. Keil and Delitzsch give the sense as help or deliverance, or, taking the abstract for the concrete, a helper.

The father named in the title occupies Henry and Clarke. Henry notes that surnames were taken then as now, some from a place and some from a parent, and used where the eminence of the parents brought honour; but he calls it a groundless conceit of the Jews that where the father of a prophet is named he also was a prophet. He allows himself one turn on the name, that Beeri signifies a well, which may put us in mind of the fountain of living waters from which prophets are drawn and must be continually drawing. Clarke collects the traditions instead: that Epiphanius made him a man of Belemoth in the tribe of Issachar, which Clarke thinks no other than Beelmeon toward Esdraelon; and that the rabbins name Bura as his father, a prince of the tribe of Reuben at the time when Tiglath-pileser carried some of the tribes into captivity, which would make the prophet a native of Beelmeon beyond Jordan. Clarke settles only that he lived in the kingdom of Samaria, his prophecies for the most part having a view to that state. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by another road: he prophesied not only concerning but in the kingdom of the ten tribes, so that he must be regarded as a subject of it, and this is favoured not merely by the occupation of his addresses but by the peculiar style and language of his prophecies, which have here and there an Aramaean colouring.

The four kings of Judah set a problem in arithmetic, and Clarke and Calvin both work it. Clarke counts a hundred and twelve years from the beginning of the reign of Uzziah to the end of that of Hezekiah, and observes that if the prophet was twenty or five and twenty when he began, he must have lived a hundred and thirty-seven years; even allowing ten years at each end during which he may not have prophesied, a hundred and fifteen remain. He adds that nothing in the whole collection proves he prophesied so long. Calvin works from the other direction. Uzziah, also called Azariah, reigned fifty-two years but abdicated his royal dignity after being smitten with leprosy, so that his son succeeded him; and since Uzziah began to reign in the twenty seventh year of Jeroboam the son of Joash, Hosea must have prophesied some thirty-six years under him, and began some years before the end of the reign of Jeroboam, so that forty at least appear. Calvin doubts whether the years of Jotham should be counted from the leprosy of his father or from his death, and reckons that more than forty-five years had passed before the next king began to reign.

On the authority of the book both Gill and Henry are brief. Gill takes the opening as the general title of the whole, showing its divine original and authority: the word was brought to the prophet by the Spirit of God, impressed upon his mind, and committed to him to be delivered unto others. Henry says it was to him, and came with power and efficacy, revealed as a real thing and not a fancy or imagination of his own, so that what he said and wrote was by divine inspiration, as Paul speaks of what he had.
2:
The opening phrase is read three ways. Gill takes it to mean only that what follows is the first part of this prophecy, and denies the larger claims: the prophet was not the first to whom the word of the Lord came, since Moses and Samuel and David were before him, nor the first of the minor prophets, since some place Jonah and Amos earlier. Henry allows a wider sense, that it may refer to the set of prophets raised up about this time, among whom Hosea was the first to foretell the destruction of Israel, though he prefers to refer it to the prophecies of Hosea themselves. Keil and Delitzsch render it literally, at the commencement of the speaking of Jehovah, and insist the verb is a perfect and not an infinitive; Ellicott gives the same sense.

All remark the harshness of a first commission. Gill observes that the prophet was put upon hard service at once, in a manner that must have been disagreeable to a young man. Henry says he might have wished to be excused from dealing so roughly until he had gained authority and some interest in their affections, and that the task was harder for his being first, with none raised up to second him; but he must begin here, that they might know what to expect from a prophet of the Lord, and must not only preach it but write and publish it as a witness against them. Calvin puts it most strongly. The prophet begins not with smooth things, nor gently exhorts to repentance, nor takes a circuitous course to soften the asperity of his doctrine, but is sent like a herald to proclaim war. Calvin draws the inference that the diseases of the people were incurable, since God is not wont to deal so severely, and that the prophet was sent when the state of things was almost past recovery.

The marriage divides them. Ellicott states the question at length: is it a historic occurrence, the only too real tragedy of the personal experience of the author, or is the chapter a merely allegorical representation designed to exhibit the moral condition of Israel in vivid colours? Able writers have advocated each of these opposed theories, and he judges the balance of evidence to incline to the historic. He raises a second question, whether Gomer was guilty before the marriage or after, and prefers the latter, since the former involves the harshness of conceiving such a marriage as the result of a divine command. On his reading the wickedness which after marriage revealed itself to the agonised heart of the prophet was transfigured into an emblem of the wrong done to Jehovah by his nation, so that his past came before him in a changed aspect and the purpose which shaped his sorrowful career was interpreted to him as a command. Wesley takes the other side without argument, holding that it was probably done in vision and proposed parabolically to the people, as David considered the parable of Nathan.

Who the wife stands for is agreed. Clarke reports Newcome that she is a wife from among a people remarkable for spiritual fornication, and observes that God calls himself the husband of Israel, so that the chosen nation owed him the fidelity of a wife; the command is spoken with indignation, to join in marriage with one of those who have committed fornication against him and raise up children who by the power of example will themselves swerve to idolatry. Keil and Delitzsch say the marriage sets forth that the kingdom has fallen away from the Lord its God and is sunken in idolatry, and that the names of the children are so appointed as to point out the evil fruits of that departure. Wesley reads one clause practically, that the prophet is to receive and maintain the children she had before.
3:
Whether the prophet actually married is settled here in opposite directions. Clarke says all this appears to be a real transaction, though having a typical meaning, and adds that a wife taken from among that people must necessarily have been an idolatress who had worshipped the calves of Jeroboam at Dan or at Bethel. Calvin denies it flatly. God ordered the prophet to take a wife of whoredoms, but this was not actually done, for what other effect could it have had than to render the prophet contemptible and reduce his authority to nothing; the intent was to show by such a representation that they vaunted themselves without reason. He suggests that the prophet laid masses of figs before them in place of a wife, proceeding as mathematicians do when they describe their figures, and repeats that he does not believe the prophet entered a brothel to take a wife. Gill leaves both doors open, the woman being either a notorious person named in the course of prophesying or a fictitious name representing their case.

The two names are read for their sense. Gill takes the first to signify both consummation and consumption, so that she is so called either for her consummate beauty, or for her consummate wickedness, or because her ruin was inevitable, a fit emblem of the condition of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch, noting that the name occurs elsewhere only for a people, take it in a passive sense as perfection or completion and expressly deny that it indicates destruction or death: the woman was thoroughly perfected in her whoredom. Ellicott gives the sense as complete or perfect, and says it is not easy to determine whether the reference is to beauty or to character. On the second name Gill offers a man, a woman, or a place, and gives the meaning as a cake of dried figs, delicious eating in that country, pointing to the luxury that caused both sin and ruin; Keil and Delitzsch agree, and read the phrase as meaning one given over to delights.

The name given the first child is read for its sound and its history. Gill reports interpreters who make it the seed of God or the arm of God, but prefers the sense that God will sow or scatter; Clarke agrees, and points to the dispersion under Shalmaneser. Calvin allows the allusion to sowing and seed but looks further: he hears the affinity between the name of the child and the name of the nation, and takes the point to be that they were wholly degenerate, not the true nor the genuine offspring of Abraham. Ellicott notes the same resemblance in sound and adds the associations of the place, a fertile plain many times the scene of terrible struggles and a town associated with the murder of Naboth. Keil and Delitzsch insist the appellative meaning is not in view here at all, but the historical importance of the plain. On whose blood is meant, Clarke follows Newcome in referring it not to the vengeance of Jehu upon that house but to his own acts of cruelty while he resided there, and Wesley traces the sentence through the reigns that followed to the conspiracy in which the last of the line was slain.

The bow is agreed to stand for the whole. Keil and Delitzsch call it a synecdochical epithet for the military force on which the continued existence of the kingdom depended, and refer the day named not to the overthrow of the house of Jehu but to the breaking up of the kingdom which followed it. Calvin makes the same grammatical point and adds a pastoral one: the people were so inflated with their present good fortune that they laughed at the judgment denounced, thinking themselves unassailable because well furnished with arms and men and money, and the verse is meant to break down that false confidence.
6:
Even the sex of the child is read for meaning. Gill reports Kimchi taking the daughter to denote the weaker state of the kingdom afterwards, when one king reigned six months and his successor one. The name itself is agreed in sense and disputed in shade. Clarke renders it as not having obtained mercy, calls it a prophetic or typical name, and refers the whole to the total destruction of that kingdom. Ellicott renders it unloved, or perhaps unpitied, and hears in it the growing despondency of the prophet about the future of his country; he also repunctuates the rest of the verse to read that God will no longer have pity on the house of Israel, that he should indeed forgive them. Calvin weighs the verb, which means to pity and also to love, the second sense derived from the first, since it is not simply to love but to show gratuitous favour. By the name God intimates that his favour is now taken away, and the people are like a daughter whom her father casts away and disowns as unworthy of his favour. Calvin marks the progression between the two names as well: the first had said they were from the beginning degenerate, spurious children born of a harlot, since a brothel is not the house of Abraham nor the house of Abraham a brothel, but this second is a more disgraceful name still.

The mercy shown to the other kingdom is read as an aggravation. Gill takes it of the two tribes which retained the true worship, spared longer than the ten and returned after seventy years, and reads it as an aggravation of the punishment of the rest, showing that God makes a reserve of some when he rejects others. Clarke says the kingdom was spared as a kingdom after the other had been carried away. Calvin uses the verse to confirm that this prophet was appointed specifically to the northern kingdom, and refuses to let the honour stand as a verdict on the southern one. Isaiah could say of the house of Judah that its tables were full of vomiting, that they were drunken, and that contempt of God and all impiety reigned there; and though the outward worship continued at Jerusalem, and the temple was free from superstition under some of the kings named in the title, the morals of the people were very corrupt. Their conduct was nothing better than that of the Israelites, and the prophet dignifies them so highly only because he institutes a comparison for the sake of his own hearers, setting the worship at Jerusalem against the fictitious worship he was sent to condemn.

The manner of the deliverance is read in one event. Clarke says the promise was remarkably fulfilled in the supernatural defeat of the Assyrian army, so that they were saved not by bow nor sword nor battle nor horses nor horsemen, and suggests the phrase may mean not in war by horses yoked to chariots, nor by cavalry, however efficient such troops might then have been deemed. Ellicott agrees the verse was literally fulfilled in the destruction of the army of Sennacherib, and adds that the prophetic outlook anticipates a later restoration by the divine hand taking the form of mercy and forgiveness. Wesley reads the preservation as extending through the captivity, so that violence should not swallow them up nor length of exile wear them out, and the remnant should return and be planted in their own land. Keil and Delitzsch take the point of the contrast to be the removal of all false trust: since deliverance is promised to the one house through Jehovah its God, the other is to learn that he is no longer its own God, the emphasis of the phrase showing that the covenant with the idolatrous race has been dissolved.
8:
The weaning is the crux, and the voices divide sharply. Calvin sets aside as frigid the allegorical reading that the people would for a time be deprived of prophecies and priesthood and other spiritual gifts, and finds in it instead the patience of God: before utterly casting them away the Lord waited for their repentance, if indeed there was any hope for it, and only when he found them ever like themselves did he proceed to the last punishment. Henry reads it the same way, noticing the delay in the birth of the child that was to carry the presage of utter rejection, and taking it to intimate the patience of God and his unwillingness to proceed to extremity. Keil and Delitzsch name Calvin and reject him: if the weaning is mentioned with a deliberate meaning and not merely to vary the expression, it cannot indicate continued patience with a rebellious nation but rather implies the uninterrupted succession of the calamities set forth by the names of the children, so that as soon as the Lord ceases to compassionate them the state of rejection ensues. Gill sets out three possibilities, the deprivation of word and ordinances compared to milk and breasts, the forbearance of God for some forty years after the kingdom ceased in the house of Jehu, or, as he prefers, the taking away of part of the land as a child is taken from its mother, in the carrying off of the inhabitants of Gilead and Galilee and Naphtali.

Henry hears something else in the second birth. The children who carried these direful omens were all born of the harlot the prophet married, which intimates that the ruin of the people was the natural product of their sin: had they not first revolted they would never have been rejected, since God never leaves any till they first leave him. He reports also the reading of the Chaldee paraphrase, that the bearing of another son signifies their persisting in wickedness, lust still conceiving and bringing forth sin, so that they were old in adulteries and obstinate.

Clarke raises a textual difficulty in the clause that follows. The word God is not added there by any of the ancient versions or manuscripts, yet the construction absolutely requires it, and Houbigant thinks the present reading a corruption of the word meaning your God. Clarke finds it strange that no variant occurs in any manuscript yet discovered, notes that two of his oldest leave a blank of half a line after the last word, as the printed Bibles do, though the sense is not complete, and suggests that the phrase points back to the name given at the bush.

What the last name does is agreed to be final. Gill reports Aben Ezra applying it to children born in captivity who never returned, but takes it of the ten tribes themselves. Ellicott calls the child the type of utter and final repudiation, and observes that the episode is in some particulars the model for a chapter of Ezekiel. Wesley says they were once a peculiar people and are so no more, cast off as they deserved, God being no more a God to them than to any of the heathen nations. Calvin marks the three names as an ascending series: they had been called by the first, then the second testified that God was alienated from them, and now the third is more grievous still, for God in a manner abolishes the covenant made with the holy fathers, so that they cease to have any preeminence and differ nothing from the profane Gentiles. He adds the warning he draws from it, that the kingdom was then opulent, and the prophet denies those who flourished in strength and power and riches to be the people of God, so that there is no reason for hypocrites to felicitate themselves in prosperity.
10:
The promise is felt as a contradiction of what has just been said, and each voice resolves it differently. Keil and Delitzsch state the difficulty plainly: it might appear as though the promise made to the patriarchs of an innumerable increase were abolished by the rejection just predicted, and this appearance might confirm the ungodly in their false security; it is met by a proclamation of salvation which must be connected with the preceding announcement of punishment by a nevertheless. They note the almost verbal agreement between this announcement and the patriarchal promises, which naturally suggests that all the descendants of Jacob as a whole are meant, but they check that inference against the second clause, where those called not my people are the very ones who will be called sons of the living God. Ellicott marks the same thing in one line, an abrupt transition from dark presage to bright anticipation, the covenant blessings promised to Abraham yet to be realised.

Calvin reads the verse as an answer to an objection. Hypocrites had it always ready when the prophets denounced destruction, that God would be unfaithful if he did not save them: arrogating to themselves the title of the Church, they concluded that it would be impossible for them to perish, since God had promised that his Church should stand for ever and cannot deny himself. What they took as granted was just where they were deceived, for they usurped the title while alienated from God, being covenant breakers who had divorced themselves from him. The prophet, having to do with proud men who were wont to arraign the justice of God, answers that when the Lord cuts them off this promise given to Abraham will still remain safe, that his seed should be as the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.

Who the innumerable are is the remaining question. Gill denies that the fulfilment came at the return from the captivity, when some of the ten tribes went back with the others, as Theodoret and others think, since those who then returned were but few. He refers it rather to the first times of the Gospel, when multitudes from various parts of the world were converted at the day of Pentecost, and greater numbers still were met with in the ministry of the word among the dispersed, to whom Peter and James wrote their epistles; and he includes with them the Gentiles everywhere effectually called by grace, who were true Israelites and the spiritual seed. Clarke reaches the same place by a shorter road: though God had thinned and scattered them for their iniquities, the spirit and design of his promise and covenant shall be fulfilled and an Israel there shall be, whether the converted people themselves or the Gentiles now become the true Israel. Wesley is briefest and most decided, that it is not Israel after the flesh nor those very families that are carried captive, and that in the places where a people dwelt who were not his people there shall be a people of God; he takes the title of the living God to mean the fountain of life to all his children, who enables them to offer living sacrifices.
11:
The gathering is read at two levels, and most voices take both. Gill denies the fulfilment at the return from the Babylonish captivity, since only the two tribes came back in a body and few of the others; he offers instead the first times of the Gospel, when the Galileans who inhabited the countries where some of the tribes had dwelt were gathered to Christ by his ministry and those in Jerusalem and Judea who believed united with them, or else the death of Christ, by which the whole Israel of God scattered abroad was gathered together in one and Jews and Gentiles made one new man. Wesley keeps both senses side by side, an historical one referring to the return out of Babylon and a spiritual one referring to a more glorious deliverance from a more miserable captivity, so that the going up is literally out of Babylon and spiritually out of captivity to sin and to Satan. Clarke observes that after the return the distinction between the two peoples was entirely destroyed and all were included under one denomination.

The one head is identified accordingly. Clarke allows Zerubbabel their leader, and afterwards Ezra and Nehemiah, but in the more extensive view of the prophet he takes it for Christ, under whom the true Israel of Jews and Gentiles shall finally be gathered, so that there shall be one flock and one Shepherd. Wesley makes the same double identification, and adds that as the first was appointed by a foreign king yet with the full approbation of the people, so Christ is appointed head by the Father and heartily accepted by believers. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase differently, hearing behind it the departure of the twelve tribes out of Egypt: the words about appointing a head recall the rebellious congregation that was about to appoint itself a head in order to return, and so point back to Moses. They draw an inference from the union itself, that it presupposes the southern kingdom finding itself in the same situation as the northern, that is, rejected by the Lord as well.

Ellicott takes the going up as a military phrase, frequently occurring in Scripture to denote the marching forth to war, and denies that the word for the land refers to exile in any foreign country, holding that Palestine is evidently meant. On his reading the envy between the two shall cease, a world-wide dominion be established under the restored theocracy, and the true Israel, having chosen their true king, demonstrate the greatness of the day named; the brothers and sisters will then drop the curse involved in their names and recognise the divine proprietorship of Jehovah and the abundance of his pity.

Calvin insists on the order of the two verses. The one before spoke of the universal gathering of the Church, but this confines the address to the natural race of Abraham, because God commenced a restoration with that people when he extended his hand to bring the miserable exiles back to their own country. He complains that interpreters confound these things and make no distinctions, when the prophet has not mingled the two peoples with the Gentiles except for a certain purpose; the honour is claimed by no merit of theirs, but God would not make void his covenant, having chosen them to be the first-begotten. Clarke ends on the name of the child, alluding to its meaning as the seed of God: he who dispersed and sowed them in different lands shall gather them, and what was a wonderful seed time in divine justice shall be a wonderful harvest in divine mercy, sown among the nations in wrath and reaped in bounty. Wesley says the same more shortly, that the seed is now sown in the earth and buried under the clods, but great shall be its day when the harvest comes.
